problem_shape: These papers belong together because they all ask how a display can make the eye receive the intended light, not merely show an image on a flat panel. In VR and AR, the display is part of the optical system. It may need to place light at different apparent depths, make a transparent glass sheet reconstruct a full-color 3D image, create bright points floating in a real volume, keep a remote avatar lit like the local room, or preserve visible detail while the display surface changes shape. The shared pressure is that the viewer judges the final light field, color, depth cue, brightness, and motion, while the hardware can only control limited things: laser power, phase patterns, surface grooves, scanning mirrors, LED strips, headset cameras, or a small number of path-traced samples. The family is therefore about translating a desired experience into physical light commands. A paper is not only drawing pixels. It is deciding which pieces of light must be sent, delayed, bent, sampled, colored, or refreshed so the viewer's eye gets a coherent scene.
naive_failure: A smart beginner might treat the display as a normal screen: render a sharp RGB image, send it to the device, and expect the viewer to see the intended scene. That fails because these devices do not simply copy pixel values into the eye. A holographic display must control wave interference, so depth, view change, focus blur, and glossy reflections depend on how light waves combine. A transparent surface-relief hologram must work across colors while staying see-through. A volumetric laser display must put enough bright points in space without exceeding hardware and safety limits. A spinning shape-changing display must keep pixel spacing stable while its surface area expands. A headset avatar system must separate body motion, surface color, shine, and room lighting. Plain image rendering ignores the optical and physical path between command and perception.
mathematical_principle: The recurring mathematical idea is controlled mapping from desired perception to limited device actions. The method starts with a target: a color the viewer should judge as correct, a 3D image reconstructed from glass, a bright volume point, a relightable avatar, a moving afterimage surface, or a hologram with natural depth cues. It then asks what device settings could produce that target after physics gets involved. What is adjusted varies by paper: color coordinates and laser illumination in PAColorHolo, shallow surface patterns and frequency bands in the invisible holographic window, synchronized beam paths in the dual-path volumetric display, angular speed, pole height, strip length, and refresh columns in MorphSkein, or avatar shape, shine, diffuse color, and surrounding light in EgoRelight. What counts as wrong is also concrete: color mismatch, crosstalk between color channels, dim or sparse volume points, lost pixel density, broken shape fidelity, or an avatar that does not match the observed headset view. The tradeoff is accuracy versus device bandwidth and refresh speed. The math measures those errors, then changes the controllable settings while respecting optical, geometric, timing, and hardware limits.
why_math_matters: The math matters because displays exploit regular structure in light and motion. Light waves interfere in predictable ways: if the phase pattern is chosen carefully, the viewer sees a depth cue instead of a flat patch. Different colors travel through diffractive structures differently, so a full-color transparent hologram needs frequency separation, meaning putting different color instructions into different spatial bands so they do not corrupt each other. Laser-excited volume displays need coordinated scanning because brightness and point density come from where beams meet space over time. Persistence of vision, meaning the eye blends fast repeated flashes into a continuous image, lets MorphSkein use spinning LED strips as a surface, but only if the release of rows and columns matches the changing troposkein shape. Headset relighting works because shine changes with view and light while diffuse surface color is more stable. These are not decorative equations. They are the bookkeeping rules that connect a device command to what the eye finally sees.
paper_family: The representative papers are versions of the same deeper move: turn a desired visual experience into a device-specific light plan. PAColorHolo starts from the fact that holographic color is distorted by lasers, spatial light modulators, lens color errors, and camera response, so it learns and controls a color mapping that better matches human judgment. The invisible holographic window works from the opposite physical object: a transparent glass surface must remain transmissive while still reconstructing a full-color 3D image, so it uses shallow sinusoidal relief and spatial-frequency band division rather than three separate color holograms. HoloPathTracer connects display design to light transport by solving ordinary scene light paths and wave propagation together, so phase-only holograms can preserve focus cues and material effects. The dual-path volumetric display uses synchronized lasers, modulators, mirrors, and a varifocal lens to raise brightness and point density in physical space. MorphSkein treats a spinning changing surface as the display, preserving density by releasing rows and rendering extra columns as area grows. EgoRelight is the social VR branch: capture, relight, and integrate a user from a headset view.
what_changed: The 2026 version of this family seems less satisfied with flat-image quality and more concerned with the whole perception pipeline. The evidence emphasizes depth cues, parallax, focus, color fidelity, transparent display surfaces, room-light-visible volumetric graphics, relightable avatars, and shape-changing displays that preserve density. Another change is that hardware and computation are treated as one design problem. PAColorHolo adjusts color and illumination around device distortions. HoloPathTracer joins scene light paths with wave propagation. The invisible window changes the surface profile to improve transmittance. The dual-path display doubles and coordinates optical paths. MorphSkein changes both geometry and refresh behavior. The family is moving from showing images toward controlling physical light delivery.
limits: These papers depend on device assumptions that may not transfer. PAColorHolo needs the display, camera response, lasers, and viewer study conditions to match its color model. The invisible holographic window trades full-color transparency for a reduced viewing angle and depends on manufacturable surface relief. HoloPathTracer reports simulations and prototype validation, but practical holographic displays still face computation and hardware constraints. The dual-path volumetric display uses femtosecond lasers, synchronized optics, an Xe-filled volume, and safety controls. MorphSkein assumes ideal troposkein geometry; wrong angular speed, motor limits, MCU speed, or LED refresh can reduce density and shape fidelity. EgoRelight depends on headset camera views, learned appearance behavior, and recoverable room lighting. The evidence does not prove universal performance across all users, rooms, content, devices, or long deployments.
